title: The 60-Minute Project Kick-Off That Saves You Six Months of Arguments
author: Nick Martin
summary: Nick Martin argues that most arguments in month four of a project trace back to four questions nobody asked at the kick-off, and he offers a 60-minute meeting structure that settles them in week one. He opens with a client whose 90-minute kick-off gave 60 minutes to presenting the plan and 5 to questions, only for the sponsor and project lead to discover months later that they disagreed about whether a dashboard covered six regions or two. Untangling it cost roughly 900 hours against twelve person-hours for the meeting. His five steps are writing a shared done sentence, building a decision list with one named decider each, running a pre-mortem, writing a not-doing list the sponsor endorses aloud, and locking in names and dates with a booked two-week check-in. Each step comes with the exact words a facilitator can say. He also answers the objection that this starts arguments early, and he advises giving a launch-minded sponsor five minutes up front and moving the plan walkthrough to a separate briefing.
points: The done sentence is written individually before anyone shares, which exposes the three or four different versions of the project in the room before the first answer anchors everyone.
Every item on the decision list gets exactly one name, and if the room offers two names the decision is not yet made.
Running the pre-mortem before the not-doing list surfaces scope worries nobody planned to mention, and each of the top three risks gets an owner and a first action this month.
Having the sponsor agree the not-doing column out loud gives the team a ready answer when someone asks to add something in month three.
Booking the two-week check-in before anyone leaves the room is what makes follow-through actually happen.
quotes: Most arguments in Month 4 of a project come from four questions nobody asked at the kick-off.
The plan had taken two weeks to build, and it got 60 of those minutes. The last 5 minutes were “Any questions?” There weren’t any.
Everyone writes their own answer before anyone hears anyone else’s. That way you hear the real differences before the first answer sets the tone for everyone else.
Most month-four standoffs are two people who both thought a call was theirs. This step names one person per decision before that can happen.
People already know how the project will go wrong. The pre-mortem gives them permission to say it.
A kick-off is supposed to build momentum, and the done sentence will surface disagreement immediately. But the disagreement already exists. Better to get it out now as opposed to later.
Most project arguments are predictable. They’re about the same four things. So why do we keep waiting until month four to have them?
